111	DAF is well-defined when $\Delta_{\text{full}} > 0$; in our data, the minimum per-task $\Delta_{\text{full}}$ is $+9.58$ (\texttt{find-non-living-thing}), ensuring numerical stability. Since DAF $= \delta P / (\delta P + \Delta_{\text{nd}})$, it increases monotonically with $P$---a mathematical consequence, not an empirical finding. DAF should therefore be interpreted relative to the environment's penalty magnitude: it quantifies the penalty's amplification of death asymmetry, not a universal constant. We report both DAF at the environment default ($P{=}100$) and the penalty-independent death-asymmetry label fraction (78.9\%) as complementary metrics.

48	A potential concern is oracle circularity: whether episode-level labels reflect tie-breaking artifacts rather than genuine modality differences. We audit all 245 labels. Of the 150 \texttt{no\_preference} labels (61.2\%), 115 (46.9\%) are both-alive ties and 35 (14.3\%) are both-dead---all excluded from router training. The remaining 95 training labels are entirely genuine: 75 from death asymmetry (70 deterministic-preferred, 5 internal-preferred) and 20 from score comparison with both strategies surviving (16 deterministic-preferred, 4 internal-preferred). Zero labels depend on tie-breaking. Retraining the router using only death-asymmetry labels yields step-level balanced accuracy of 57.3\%, within 1$\sigma$ of the full-label retrain (57.6 $\pm$ 0.5\%, step-level Trainer evaluation); score-comparison labels contribute negligible additional signal. (Step-level metrics are used here for the relative comparison; as shown in \S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}, absolute generalization to new episodes is near chance.) The 97.4\% step-level tie rate (\S\ref{sec:collection}) further motivates episode-level over step-level labeling.

222	\paragraph{Per-task-type evaluation breakdown.} To test whether the router learns transferable routing strategies or merely task-type classification, we evaluate existing checkpoints (8 seeds) separately on each of the 11 task types. Of the 11 task types, 7 have \emph{all-deterministic} labels (no internal-preferred episodes exist), making balanced accuracy undefined---the router has nothing to learn beyond the trivial always-deterministic default. For the remaining 4 task types where both classes are present, balanced accuracy ranges from 50.0\% to 73.0\%, but this apparent signal does not indicate cross-task-type routing transfer: the router is effectively classifying task types (which correlate with death risk) rather than extracting a generalizable routing strategy. This complements the data scaling ablation: routing signal does not transfer across task types because the signal \emph{is} the task type---whether a given task carries death risk. The 4B capacity scaling result (Appendix~\ref{app:ablations}) suggests capacity is one factor, but even 4B's $59.0\%$ episode-level accuracy does not demonstrate cross-task-type transfer.

tool_args.old_string: We probe whether counterfactual labels can train a step-level router, as a diagnostic of label informativeness. An implicit router (Qwen3-1.7B fine-tuned; Appendix~\ref{app:router-details}) yields $54.1 \pm 5.4\%$ step-level balanced accuracy but $47.1 \pm 2.2\%$ on held-out episodes (8 seeds), below always-deterministic (50\%). A controlled replication using identical 4-seed configurations for all three scales yields 0.6B: $50.7\%$, 1.7B: $43.1 \pm 1.0\%$, 4B: $59.0\%$, confirming non-monotonic (U-shaped) capacity scaling. The 1.7B dip is robust across seeds (range $41.7$--$44.4\%$), ruling out the prior configuration confound. This non-monotonic pattern, combined with universally low internal recall, reinforces that learned routing does not scale predictably with capacity at current data scales. Only 4B exceeds the baseline ($58.96 \pm 1.94\%$, $p < 0.005$; Appendix~\ref{app:ablations}). Augmentation-based data scaling ($25\%$--$800\%$) provides no improvement (Appendix~\ref{app:seed-robustness}), but paraphrase augmentation inflates the majority class (89.6\%$\rightarrow$97.7\%) without generating novel routing patterns; real-data scaling (requiring ${\sim}1{,}350$ episode pairs for 50 minority-class examples) remains an open question. Capacity scaling improves episode-level routing ($+9$\,pp at 4B) without improving step-level accuracy (flat ${\sim}53\%$); the extractable signal is task-type-level structure. The cost of this extraction (4B for $+9$\,pp) is consistent with our analytical methodology being more efficient than brute-force learned routing. Deployed end-to-end (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}), the router ($-10.70$) does not outperform always-deterministic ($-9.47$; overlapping CIs). Label quality is verified in Appendix~\ref{app:labeling}.
tool_args.new_string: We probe whether counterfactual labels can train a step-level router, as a diagnostic of label informativeness. An implicit router (Qwen3, LoRA fine-tuned; Appendix~\ref{app:router-details}) is trained at three scales (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B) with identical 4-seed configurations. Step-level balanced accuracy is flat across scales ($56.4 \pm 3.5\%$, $58.2 \pm 4.0\%$, $59.2 \pm 3.5\%$; all within seed variance), indicating step-level discrimination is not capacity-sensitive. At episode level, only 4B exceeds the always-deterministic baseline ($59.0 \pm 1.9\%$, $p < 0.005$; Appendix~\ref{app:ablations}), while 0.6B ($50.7 \pm 2.6\%$) and 1.7B ($43.1 \pm 1.0\%$) remain at or below chance. The 1.7B dip is robust across seeds (range $41.7$--$44.4\%$); this non-monotonic pattern, combined with universally low internal recall, reinforces that learned routing does not scale predictably with capacity at current data scales. Augmentation-based data scaling ($25\%$--$800\%$) provides no improvement (Appendix~\ref{app:seed-robustness}), but paraphrase augmentation inflates the majority class (89.6\%$\rightarrow$97.7\%) without generating novel routing patterns; real-data scaling (requiring ${\sim}1{,}350$ episode pairs for 50 minority-class examples) remains an open question. Capacity scaling improves episode-level routing ($+9$\,pp at 4B) without improving step-level accuracy (flat ${\sim}57\%$); the extractable signal is task-type-level structure. The cost of this extraction (4B for $+9$\,pp) is consistent with our analytical methodology being more efficient than brute-force learned routing. Deployed end-to-end (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}), the router ($-10.70$) does not outperform always-deterministic ($-9.47$; overlapping CIs). Label quality is verified in Appendix~\ref{app:labeling}.

115	\label{app:router-details}
116	
117	We use Qwen3-1.7B for the router to avoid circular dependency with the Qwen2.5-7B data-generating model.
118	
119	With gradient accumulation of 1 (effective batch size 4), routing performance is highly sensitive to the evaluation split; this suggests overfitting to specific train/validation partition boundaries. With gradient accumulation of 8 (effective batch size 32), step-level performance stabilizes across splits (${\sim}54\%$ balanced accuracy). All reported results use gradient accumulation 8.
120	
121	Under step-level evaluation with a fixed data split, cross-seed balanced accuracy ranges from 52.7\% to 58.1\%, but internal recall varies from 51.5\% to 81.8\%, reflecting threshold sensitivity. However, episode-level evaluation reveals that this apparent discrimination does not generalize: balanced accuracy drops to $47.1 \pm 2.2\%$ across 8 cross-split seeds (Appendix~\ref{app:seed-robustness}). Deployed end-to-end, the trained router allocates 97.0\% of episodes to deterministic computation with 17.6\% death rate, and misrouting cost (death from internally-routed episodes) exceeds the benefit of correctly routing rare internal-preferred cases.
122	
123	\paragraph{Evaluation methods.} All results use \emph{generation-based evaluation}: the model generates a routing label as text (\texttt{enable\_thinking=False}), parsed for classification. We evaluate at two granularities: \emph{step-level} (steps from the same episode may appear in both train and validation sets) and \emph{episode-level} (entire episodes held out). Step-level accuracy ($54.1 \pm 5.4\%$) exceeds chance, indicating the router captures some signal, but episode-level accuracy ($47.1 \pm 2.2\%$, below chance) shows this does not generalize to unseen episodes.
